title: Lesson 78: Workflow Engines vs Agents: When to Use Deterministic Orchestration
description: Separating code-controlled workflows from model-controlled agents, what durable execution actually guarantees, applying the five-question test, and placing one bounded agentic step inside a deterministic skeleton.

questions.question: A process has steps you can enumerate, a bounded step count, and a validator that can judge each step's output. Which shape fits?
options: An autonomous agent, because the number of items varies from batch to batch
An orchestrator that discovers its own subtasks per run with no fixed outer structure
A workflow, because the steps are enumerable and code can gate whether each one succeeded
A workflow only if no model is used anywhere, since any model call would break determinism
questions.explanation: When code can name the steps and a validator can decide success, determinism is a feature. A model may still do real work inside a workflow, but it never chooses the next step.

questions.question: You place an agent as one step inside a durable workflow. What must the seam define before the first run?
options: Typed input and output schemas, validation, an idempotency key, a timeout, a cost ceiling, and an escalation
An unbounded iteration budget so that the agent can always finish, plus a logged transcript kept for audit purposes
Direct access to the workflow event history so the engine can replay the agent's reasoning later
A shared prompt registry so the deterministic engine can cache the model result on every replay
questions.explanation: The engine only sees the validated result or a failure it can route, so the seam needs explicit contracts. Every undefined item, from the idempotency key to the cost ceiling, becomes an incident later.

questions.question: Why must a model call never sit inside deterministic workflow code?
options: Because the model would cost more than a plain function call and inflate the overall run budget
Because the workflow is replayed to rebuild state, and a fresh model answer breaks that match
Because workflow engines cannot serialize a model response into their event history
Because the model needs network access, which the engine always blocks for security
questions.explanation: Durable workflow code is re-run to reconstruct state from the recorded history. A model call returns a different answer on replay, so the history no longer matches the code; the model belongs in an activity or step.
